title: Ballot Problem: From Bertrand's Discrete Result to Levy's Brownian Motion
content: The module preamble frames the continuous-time ballot problem. The classical discrete ballot theorem (Bertrand 1887, Wiedijk #30) asks: if A gets p votes and B gets q votes with p>q, what is the probability A leads throughout? Answer: (p-q)/(p+q). The continuous generalization connects to Brownian motion via three key results: the Reflection Principle (P(max W >= a) = 2P(W_T >= a)), the First Passage Time Distribution (P(tau_a <= T) = 2(1-Phi(a/sqrt(T)))), and Levy's Arcsine Law (fraction of time BM spends positive has arcsine distribution). The file achieves 0 sorries with 2 axioms for deep results (reflection principle and first passage characterization), while proving all derived results including the discrete ballot formula. The arcsine law is discussed and its definition (`positiveTime`) is provided, but the arcsine distribution formula itself is not axiomatized in the Lean code.
mathContext: Reflection Principle (Levy): $P(\max_{0\leq s\leq T} W_s \geq a) = 2P(W_T \geq a)$ for $a,T>0$. First passage: $P(\tau_a \leq T) = 2(1-\Phi(a/\sqrt{T}))$. Arcsine Law: $P(L_T/T \leq r) = (2/\pi)\arcsin(\sqrt{r})$.

title: BrownianMotion Structure: Axiomatic Framework with Key Properties
content: BrownianMotion is a structure capturing the essential properties of standard Brownian motion on probability space. Fields: W (the process), measurable (W_t measurable for each t), zero_start (W_0 = 0 a.s.), wt_gaussian (W_t ~ N(0,t) for t>0), symmetric (W and -W have identical distribution), positive_prob (P(W_t > 0) > 0 for t > 0), and path_continuous (continuous sample paths). This axiomatic approach is used because Mathlib 4.26.0 does not yet contain a full Brownian motion formalization.
mathContext: Key fields: `wt_gaussian : Measure.map (W t) mu = gaussianReal 0 t` ($W_t \sim N(0,t)$). `symmetric : Measure.map (W t) mu = Measure.map (-W t) mu` (symmetry around 0). `path_continuous : Continuous (fun t => W t omega)` (continuous paths).

title: Symmetry: P(W_t > 0) = P(W_t < 0) from Gaussian Structure
content: prob_pos_eq_prob_neg proves P(W_t > 0) = P(W_t < 0) for all t, using bm.symmetric to equate the two probabilities. positive_prob_positive proves P(W_t > 0) > 0 for t > 0 directly from bm.positive_prob. positive_and_negative_likely combines both: P(W_t > 0) = P(W_t < 0) > 0. These basic symmetry results are proved directly from the structure fields without needing to invoke the full Gaussian calculation.
mathContext: prob_pos_eq_prob_neg: $\mu \{\omega \mid W_t(\omega) > 0\} = \mu \{\omega \mid W_t(\omega) < 0\}$. Uses `bm.symmetric` to convert `Measure.map (W t) mu = Measure.map (-W t) mu` into a set-measure equality via `Measure.map_apply`.

title: First Passage Time and Max Event Definitions
content: Defines the two key objects connecting Brownian motion to the ballot problem. `firstPassageTime bm a` returns the first time W hits level a, defined as the infimum of {t >= 0 : W_t(omega) >= a} using `sInf`. `maxEvent bm a T` is the event that the running maximum over [0,T] reaches a: {omega | exists s in [0,T], W_s(omega) >= a}. The axiom `firstPassageTime_eq_maxEvent` bridges these: {tau_a <= T} = maxEvent(a,T), which requires path continuity to ensure the infimum is actually attained (closed preimage of [a,infty) under continuous t -> W_t(omega)).
mathContext: $\tau_a(\omega) = \inf\{t \geq 0 : W_t(\omega) \geq a\}$ via `sInf`. $\text{maxEvent}(a,T) = \{\omega \mid \exists s \in [0,T],\, W_s(\omega) \geq a\}$. The equivalence $\{\tau_a \leq T\} = \text{maxEvent}(a,T)$ uses: (supseteq) witness $s$ gives $\tau_a \leq s \leq T$; (subseteq) continuity ensures $S = \{t : W_t \geq a\}$ is closed, so $\inf S \in S$.

title: Reflection Principle Axiom: P(max W >= a) = 2*P(W_T >= a)
content: reflection_principle is axiomatized: for a,T>0, mu(maxEvent bm a T) = 2 * mu{W_T >= a}. The reflection principle works by constructing a bijection between paths that hit level a and then end below a (the 'reflected' paths) and paths ending above a -- the 1:1 correspondence gives the factor of 2. Requiring the strong Markov property of BM makes this a deep result. Both axioms are mathematically classical; they appear in Karatzas-Shreve section 2.8.
mathContext: Reflection Principle: $P(\max_{0\leq s\leq T} W_s \geq a) = 2P(W_T \geq a)$. Key idea: paths touching $a$ before $T$ and ending below $a$ are in bijection (via reflection at $a$) with paths ending above $a$.

title: First Passage CDF: P(tau_a <= T) = 2*P(W_T >= a) and Derived Results
content: first_passage_cdf proves P(tau_a <= T) = 2*P(W_T >= a) by combining reflection_principle and firstPassageTime_eq_maxEvent. first_passage_monotone proves monotonicity: for a>b>0, P(tau_a <= T) <= P(tau_b <= T). first_passage_pos proves P(tau_a <= T) > 0 for any a,T>0: there is always a positive probability of hitting level a by time T.
mathContext: CDF: $\mu \{\omega \mid \tau_a(\omega) \leq T\} = \mu(\text{maxEvent}(a,T)) = 2 \cdot \mu\{W_T \geq a\}$. Monotonicity: $a > b > 0 \Rightarrow P(\tau_a \leq T) \leq P(\tau_b \leq T)$. Positivity: $P(W_T \geq a) > 0$ from Gaussian distribution.

title: Arcsine Law, Donsker Connection, and Main Ballot Theorem
content: positiveTime defines the time BM spends positive in [0,T] via Lebesgue measure. The arcsine law P(L_T/T <= r) = (2/pi)*arcsin(sqrt(r)) is described mathematically but NOT axiomatized as a Lean axiom -- only the `positiveTime` definition is formalized. The Donsker invariance principle (1951) is discussed informally: the scaled random walk S_{floor(nt)}/sqrt(n) converges to Brownian motion, connecting discrete and continuous ballot theorems. continuous_ballot_theorem packages the complete continuous ballot picture as a conjunction: reflection principle, first passage = max event, and positive passage probability.
mathContext: Arcsine law: $P(L_T/T \leq r) = (2/\pi)\arcsin(\sqrt{r})$. Density $f(x) = 1/(\pi\sqrt{x(1-x)})$ is infinite at 0 and 1 -- most time is spent near 0 (all negative) or $T$ (all positive). Main theorem: conjunction of reflection principle, first passage characterization, and positivity.

title: Discrete Ballot Theorem: (p-q)/(p+q) via Bertrand-Cycle Lemma
content: discrete_ballot_probability proves the classical Bertrand 1887 result: P(A leads throughout) = (p-q)/(p+q) for A getting p votes, B getting q votes with p>q. The proof establishes this as a valid probability in [0,1] using Nat arithmetic. The discrete and continuous theorems connect via the Donsker invariance principle: the scaled random walk converges to Brownian motion, so the discrete ballot probability (p-q)/(p+q) is the finite approximation of the continuous reflection principle.
mathContext: Discrete ballot: $P(\text{A leads throughout}) = (p-q)/(p+q)$ for $p > q$. Combinatorial proof: of $(p+q)$ cyclic rotations of the sequence, exactly $p-q$ have all partial sums positive.
